title: The five in authority
hook: decisions are made through five chosen Sikhs

segments.voice: Yesterday, the jathedar: the leader of a band, and the head of a Takht who serves it. Your line was the leader of the takht. Did you lead anything as a servant of the task? Day one thousand two hundred seventy-eight.

Drums first, then flags. A street has been cleared for a nagar kirtan, a Sikh procession: families in their best clothes, a float carrying the Guru Granth Sahib under a canopy. And walking out front, ahead of everything, five Sikhs dressed alike, swords held upright. Those five lead. Count back through this block and the number keeps turning up: five who give amrit, five who hear a confession and set a tankhah. It isn't decoration. In the Sikh way of doing things, when something weighty must be decided, it goes to five. Today: the five in authority.
screen: `FIVE WALK AHEAD OF THE PROCESSION.` → `FIVE AT AMRIT, FIVE AT TANKHAH.` → `WEIGHTY THINGS GO TO FIVE.`

segments.voice: Begin where the number begins: the panj pyare, the five beloved ones at Anandpur. In the tradition's telling, the Tenth Guru not only initiated them but asked to be initiated by them, and at Chamkaur, as this path told it long ago, the five ordered the Guru to leave the fort, and he obeyed. So from the start, five chosen Sikhs could speak with an authority the Guru himself honored. The Sikh Rehat Maryada carries that into ordinary life. When amrit is given, five give it. When a breach is confessed, five decide the tankhah. Now three things about how this works. First, the five are chosen for the task, from among Sikhs who keep the code. The authority belongs to the role, not to the person's rank. A shopkeeper can be one of five, standing beside a scholar. Second, five is enough people that no single will can rule the room, and few enough that they can actually sit together and reach a decision. One person can be swayed by a grudge. A crowd can be swayed by a mood. Five have to talk. Third, the same pattern scales up. At the Akal Takht, the heads of the Takhts and senior granthis can sit together as five, the Panj Singh Sahiban, to decide matters for the whole panth. A village sangat and the throne of the Timeless use the same shape. Behind it is the conviction this block keeps returning to: the Guru is present where the Khalsa gathers. So the answer to who decides is short. Five decide.
screen: `AT CHAMKAUR, THE GURU OBEYED THE FIVE.` · `FIVE GIVE AMRIT, FIVE SET TANKHAH.` · `CHOSEN FOR THE TASK, NOT BY RANK.` · `THE SAME SHAPE AT THE AKAL TAKHT.` · then, large: `FIVE DECIDE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: decide with four others. The deciding is for later today. For now, settle, and breathe. Bring to mind one decision you've been carrying alone. A small one is fine. Then, one at a time, picture four people you trust sitting around it with you. Not to vote it away from you; to talk. Hear each of them ask you one question. Notice which question you don't want to answer. Stay with that one until the bell. The bell holds the time.
The five in authority. In Sikh practice, weighty decisions go to five chosen Sikhs, from the amrit ceremony to the Akal Takht. Today's word.
Your line: five decide. Today, take the decision you pictured to four real people, even by text, and ask each one for a single question before you choose. Day one thousand two hundred seventy-eight.

howItsDone: Sikhs bring weighty decisions to five chosen Sikhs, the panj pyare, who give amrit, set tankhah and lead processions; at the Akal Takht, the Panj Singh Sahiban decide matters for the panth.

notes: The claim that the code allows a sangat to put a question to five chosen Sikhs in the Guru's presence is a paraphrase; please confirm it is in the Sikh Rehat Maryada, or cut it.
Panj Singh Sahiban is described as the heads of the Takhts and senior granthis sitting together as five at the Akal Takht; please confirm the description.
The Chamkaur episode is told as tradition and only in brief (earlier days, including 621, told it); please confirm.
The nagar kirtan detail (five dressed alike, swords upright, barefoot, walking ahead of the Granth) is offered as a common sight; please confirm or soften 'bare feet'.
'Five is enough people that no single will can rule the room' is an interpretation, not a claim from a source.
